demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I feel isolated and set apart from others
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Physical pain in the same body parts as during the event is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being an unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, unless the patient was also physically injured during the event. That makes this item clinically implausible from the provided trauma context.

A global mistrust appraisal is a weak fit with bereavement trauma unless there is some interpersonal betrayal, negligence, or assault-related context. The rest of the profile centers on loss, alarm, and isolation rather than interpersonal threat from other people, so this item is not well supported by the trauma type or the other selected items.

For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, ambulances can plausibly cue the death context and workplace cues may be idiosyncratically linked, but 'People cycling' is hard to connect clinically unless the loved one died in a cycling-related incident, which is not reflected anywhere else in threat, appraisals, or memory. It stands out as a trigger with no supporting context in the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: The memory profile is dominated by grief-related recall and affective reliving without clear imagery, which fits bereavement trauma. 'Intense shame' on recall is not impossible, but here it lacks support from the negative appraisals, which focus on identity loss, isolation, and life destruction rather than self-blame, guilt, or humiliation. In this profile, shame is insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation and trauma type.

vignette:
Kwame Asante is a 55-year-old Ghanaian-American painter, married for nearly three decades, who presented for treatment approximately eight months after the sudden death of his adult son, Kofi. Kofi was thirty-one years old and had complained of chest tightness during a phone call with Kwame on a Tuesday evening. Kwame told him to rest, assuming it was stress. By the following morning, Kofi was dead of a massive cardiac event, discovered by his wife when she woke. Kwame received the call while standing in the parking lot of a job site, roller in hand, paint still wet on his forearms. He had not been there. He had not gone to him. That fact - ordinary and unavoidable as it was - had lodged itself at the center of everything that followed.

In the weeks after the funeral, Kwame moved through the necessary rituals of grief with a composure that those around him mistook for strength. He returned to work within ten days. He kept painting. But something had shifted in the texture of ordinary life that he could not name and could not reverse. The job site, which had once been simply where he worked, became a place threaded with unbearable association. The sound of a passing ambulance on a nearby street - a sound common to any urban work environment - would stop him mid-stroke. His chest would tighten, his hands would still, and without any coherent image forming in his mind, the full weight of that Tuesday evening would descend on him: not as a picture, but as a feeling so complete it seemed to occupy his body rather than his thoughts. He came to dread the ambulance's wail the way some men dread a particular smell or song, though he could not always explain to himself exactly why the sound hit him the way it did.

At home, the evenings became their own kind of difficulty. When the light went, something in Kwame shifted into a state of readiness he could not stand down from. He would lie beside his wife, Abena, listening to the house settle, his body taut against the mattress, as though waiting for news that had not yet arrived but was certain to. He was convinced, in a way he recognized as irrational but could not dismantle, that the darkness carried a particular danger - that the night was when things happened, when calls came, when the world rearranged itself without warning. He felt no safer in his own home than he did anywhere else; the familiarity of the rooms offered nothing. He had come to believe that safety was simply no longer something available to him.

What frightened him most, perhaps, was how unrecognizable he had become to himself. Kwame had always been a man who knew who he was - a craftsman, a father, a husband, a man of steady habits and quiet faith. He could no longer locate that person. He described himself in the intake session as feeling "hollowed out," as though the man who had answered that parking-lot phone call had not fully returned from it. Conversations in which others mentioned losing someone - a neighbor's passing, a colleague's bereavement - would cause him to withdraw into silence so complete that coworkers had begun to give him a wide berth. He had not explained himself to them, and they had stopped asking. The distance between himself and other people felt both enormous and fixed. He was certain they could not understand what he carried, and he had largely stopped trying to let them in.

Abena had finally asked him, quietly and without accusation, whether he was going to let someone help him. He had not answered her that night. But he called the clinic the following week. He arrived presenting with a PCL-5 score of 67, visibly guarded, sitting forward in his chair as though prepared to leave. What he said he wanted was to stop feeling like his life was over. What he seemed most afraid of was that it might be.
